newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba data shows German economy a bit stronger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba data shows German economy a bit stronger.

text.p: Bundesbank data released on Wednesday showed the German economy was slightly stronger in the fourth quarter than previously believed.
But economists said the picture was still not one of a vigorous recovery, and the outlook for the current quarter remained slack.

The central bank data showed a 0.1 percent rise in gross domestic product (GDP) in the fourth quarter of 1996 from the previous quarter, and 2.2 percent from the year-earlier quarter. The growth rates were calculated by Reuters from the raw data.
Previous Bundesbank data released two weeks ago had shown a 0.2 percent decline from the previous quarter and 1.6 percent year-on-year rise.
"These data show the economy was not as weak as we thought. At least now it's not a fall but a marginal rise," said economist Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS in Frankfurt.
"Still, even these numbers are highly uncertain. Seasonal adjustments are putting a bias on the data. The 2.2 percent in particular looks excessively strong," Fahrinkrug said.
Federal Statistics Office data put the fourth-quarter year-on-year rise at only 1.9 percent. The main strength of the new Bundesbank data results from downward revisions to earlier figures.

Slow growth and rising unemployment are boosting government outlays while cutting tax revenues. The squeeze fuels fear that Germany won't meet the guidelines to qualify for the planned European single currency, a prospect that could scupper the entire project, scheduled to start in January 1999.
Some economists stress that the Maastricht Treaty gives leeway on the guidelines, but German officials have been among the most dogmatic advocates of strict interpretation.

"With these figures Germany won't meet the EMU criteria perfectly, but that is enough for a start of EMU in 1999. With figures that close to the EMU criteria, EMU will go forward, said Christian Sobotta of LGT Asset Management in Frankfurt, who sees Germany's budget deficit at 3.1 percent of GDP in 1997, the key year for deciding the starting EMU members.

Many economists believe the economy remains sluggish in the current quarter, as evidenced by labour market weakness. But they say the weak mark should help fuel exports and reinforce growth starting in the second quarter.
"We may see a flat first quarter. But thereafter we see similar strength as we saw last year, particularly in exports brought on by the weaker mark," said David Brickman of Yamaichi International.
"But German consumption is particularly weak. That is something that is going to continue and offset the weaker mark," Brickman said.

Despite continued economic sluggishness, economists see almost no chance of the Bundesbank cutting interest rates soon. Price rises have accelerated in recent months, and the weak mark is a potential inflationary factor.

"The arguments in favour and against an interest rates decrease balance each other out. For the time being the Bundesbank is likely to continue its steady hand policy," said Hermann Remsperger of BHF-Bank.
The central bank holds its next policy-making council meeting on Thursday.

The GDP data came a day ahead of unemployment figures for February which economists expected to show another post-war record of 4.32 million on a seasonally-adjusted basis, up about 20,000 from January.

The Federal Statistics Office said that despite growth in the economy, the size of the German workforce declined by 491,000 in the fourth quarter compared to a year earlier, while the number of registered unemployed rose on average by 348,000.
The statistics office said that the main growth impulses in the fourth quarter came from the services sector, which grew by 4.5 percent in the fourth quarter from a year earlier.
